blocks.text: Quick verdict

Proxy-Cheap is the better choice for price-driven scraping where country or ISP targeting is enough: at its current promotional rate, 10 GB costs about $7.80 against $40 at Infatica, with no monthly plan. Infatica is the better choice when you need city or ZIP targeting, when procurement requires ethical-sourcing documentation and ISO certifications, or when you want a fully featured seven-day trial before committing. Both sell IPv6 options; Infatica's IPv6 residential pool is the more unusual product.

Infatica and Proxy-Cheap both offer residential, mobile, static ISP and datacenter proxies, including IPv6 options that few competitors sell. Their priorities differ. Infatica emphasises ethical sourcing, ISO certifications and ZIP-level targeting on every plan. Proxy-Cheap emphasises price, with rotating residential traffic currently at $0.78/GB pay-as-you-go. This comparison looks at which buyers should pay for Infatica's precision and assurances and which should take Proxy-Cheap's savings.

blocks.text: Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Proxy-Cheap in 2026: what you get

Proxy-Cheap lives up to its name: rotating residential traffic is currently advertised at $0.78/GB (70% off a $2.60 list price) with no subscription, and static ISP and datacenter IPs cost a dollar or two per month. The catalog is broad, covering IPv6 options few competitors offer, and payment by card, PayPal, Alipay or crypto is easy. The trade-offs are thinner targeting (country and ISP rather than city on rotating residential) and less published performance data than the bigger brands.

Strengths: Very low per-GB price while the promotion runs; No monthly commitment on rotating residential; Broad catalog including IPv6 and static mobile; SOCKS5 with UDP support. Weak spots: Targeting is mostly country and ISP, not city; Residential pool size not separately published; Mixed results in some independent benchmarks.
Pricing: Infatica vs Proxy-Cheap

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Proxy-Cheap's rotating residential proxies are pay-as-you-go, currently listed from $0.78/GB (a promotional price against a $2.60/GB list rate). Static residential ISP proxies start around $2.44 per IP per month, datacenter IPv4 at about $1.49, datacenter IPv6 from $0.15, and rotating mobile at $5.99/GB.

For a 10 GB month, Proxy-Cheap costs about $7.80 while Infatica costs about $40, so Proxy-Cheap saves around 80%. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $78 with Proxy-Cheap and $360 with Infatica: a 78% saving in Proxy-Cheap's favour. Both Infatica and Proxy-Cheap work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Proxy-Cheap does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Infatica lists '35M-40M' and Proxy-Cheap lists 'Not separately published (155M+ claimed across all products)'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Infatica lists 195 countries and Proxy-Cheap lists 180+. On targeting, Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP, while Proxy-Cheap offers country and ISP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times, and Proxy-Cheap offers rotating and sticky sessions. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Infatica wins. The deciding factor for Infatica: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: cheap traffic, though independent benchmark results have been mixed.
SERP and rank tracking: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results. How Proxy-Cheap compares: workable for light rank tracking at a low cost.

Social media and multi-account management: Proxy-Cheap. Proxy-Cheap has the edge here. Why: cheap static ISP and mobile IPs for persistent identities. How Infatica compares: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. How Proxy-Cheap compares: fine for country-level price checks.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Infatica wins. The deciding factor for Infatica: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: lacks city-level targeting on rotating residential.

Tight budgets: Proxy-Cheap wins. The deciding factor for Proxy-Cheap: the lowest advertised per-GB price in this pairing. The limitation on the Infatica side: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs. Verification and payment rules differ too. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Proxy-Cheap: Light; card, PayPal, Alipay and crypto accepted. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Infatica and Proxy-Cheap before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Infatica vs Proxy-Cheap faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile); Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Infatica comes out ahead in 4, Proxy-Cheap in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Infatica the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers, while Proxy-Cheap is strongest for price-sensitive scraping at moderate difficulty. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
